title: Automatic Vowel Analysis script for Praat
text:
How to use it

Open Praat
Click the “Praat” button in the upper menu
Open Praat Script
Select the script
Click the “Run” button in the upper menu
Follow the instructions provided by the script

NOTE: PRAAT TENDS TO FLICKER A LOT WITH THIS KIND OF SCRIPTS, BE CAREFUL IF YOU ARE PHOTOSENSITIVE I don’t think I can do much about it, this really is just a Praat thing. If this is a problem for your workflow, feel free to write me an email. There is technically a way to avoid the flickering, its just a bit of a pain in the ass and I cannot really do it for you in the code, I have to teach you how to bypass the buggy interface from the terminal.

title: Automatic Vowel Analysis script for Praat
text:
Additional instructions
You should have 2 folders somewhere on your PC.
The first one should contain the corpus, that is, .wav and .TextGrid files with corresponding names. The second one should be ideally empty and ready to be filled with the results generated by this script. Or you may just do it all in a single folder…
For me it’s a bit too chaotic, but if that is what you want, just input the same path twice. The script will not stand in your way.

title: Automatic Vowel Analysis script for Praat
text:
Example of use
You may try it with the example audio + TextGrid pair attached in the GitHub repository. For a bit of context, it is a young Spanish woman reading in an anechoic chamber. Her dialect employs 5 vowels /a/, /e/, /i/, /o/ and /u/. The segmentation was done automatically using MFA, so don’t expect human level precision, however, it is perfectly serviceable for this example. If you want to simulate the script analysing a whole corpus, just copy and paste the pair a few times in the same folder

title: Using Semantic Search for Dungeons and Dragons
text:
As a long time Dungeon Master, one thing I often face when introducing new players to Dungeons and Dragons is the overwhelming amount of rules involving magic. If you don’t know, every spell has quite a few specifics to it and you cannot just declare that you throw fire at your enemies. There are dice involved, measurements, sometimes material, verbal or somatic components… it is a lot… but as a new player, you often really just want to throw fire at goblins or make plants grow real fast… So I came up with an idea: What if you could just type what you want to do and my program looked up the relevant rules for you?
To do this, the question really becomes how to associate the meaning of the user input text with the meaning of what the rules say. And to answer that, we have to talk about semantic search.

title: Using Semantic Search for Dungeons and Dragons
text:
As a long time Dungeon Master, one thing I often face when introducing new players to Dungeons and Dragons is the overwhelming amount of rules involving magic. If you don’t know, every spell has quite a few specifics to it and you cannot just declare that you throw fire at your enemies. There are dice involved, measurements, sometimes material, verbal or somatic components… it is a lot… but as a new player, you often really just want to throw fire at goblins or make plants grow real fast… So I came up with an idea: What if you could just type what you want to do and my program looked up the relevant rules for you?
To do this, the question really becomes how to associate the meaning of the user input text with the meaning of what the rules say. And to answer that, we have to talk about semantic search.

title: Using Semantic Search for Dungeons and Dragons
text:
What is semantic search?
In plain English, semantic search just means searching via meaning. So how do we do that? Well first, we have to talk about how we even express meaning in a mathematical way. As humans, we understand that the meanings of ‘cats’ and ‘snakes’ are more similar to each other then the meanings of ‘cats’ and the ‘Gospel of Judas’. If a kid asked me the usual Why? question, I would say something along the lines of “Well, cats and snakes are both animals, while the Gospel of Judas is a theological text.” They would probably ask me what theological means, but that is beside the point. The relevant question for us is how can we express my answer mathematically?
We can imagine a 2d plane with the axes \(x\) and \(y\). We can say that the animalness of a concept is on the \(x\) axis while the theolgicalness lies on the \(y\) axis. So for the purpose of our example, we will place 3 concepts on this plane: Cats will go on [1,0], high on the animal axis, because, well, cats are animals and low on the theological axis because they are not really relevant for theology (I know they don’t exactly have 0 relation, but let’s keep this simple for the sake of the example.) Snakes can go at [1,0.2], because they are still very much animals, but they are a bit more connected to theology then cats. Finally, the Gospel of Judas can go to [0, 1] as it is a theological text and not an animal.









Just looking at this graph, we can see it very easily. Snakes and Cats are close to each other and both are far from the Gospel of Judas. However, Snakes are closer to the Gospel then Cats. We could even take a ruler and see the exact distances between the concepts. That is, we have just created a semantic space where concepts can be placed and the relations between their meaning become numerically measurable. In practice, we call this form of representation an Embedding Space.

Embeddings
When talking about modern AI, we often hear about tokens. You probably know that any text you feed into a large language model gets segmented into pieces which are essentially words, but not exactly. However, the reason behind this segmentation is often omitted. So, what is the deal? In short, without going too deep into how these models work on the inside (perhaps in another blog post), if we want the model to understand what we want it to do, we need to feed it meaning, not just combinations of letters. And we have already seen how meaning can be expressed mathematically.
Of course, in the real world, we wouldn’t exactly place ‘Animalness’ on the \(x\) axis, ‘Theologicalness’ on the \(y\) axis and call it a day. Real embeddings are still vectors just as the [1,0] we described before, however, they are slightly larger, as in, there are more axes. While we as humans struggle to visualise anything that has more then 3 dimensions, mathematically it is very easy to add dimensions, look: [1,0,99] This 3 dimensional vector now has one more axis, which corresponds to… I don’t know, willingness to scratch furniture. And look [1,0,99,0], a fourth dimension, this one represents the friendliness… I can keep adding them like that as long as I want to… which is sort of what happens in Natural Language Processing. The vectors we associate with each token often have thousands of dimensions and every direction in this space represents some meaning. So we end up with this high-dimensional space where concepts are placed.


Distance expression
So how do we express the distance between concepts, if there are so many dimensions we cannot visualise it? It was easy when we could use a ruler, but it gets slightly more complicated if we have to account for thousands of dimensions, right? Actually, not really. If instead of a ruler, we use maths, it is just as easy as adding more dimensions to the vector. The formula that corresponds to what a ruler would do is what we call Euclidian distance and it looks like this in 2D:
\[
d(x, y) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2}
\]
If we want to take it to 3D, all we have to do is account for the distance on the newly added \(z\) axis:
\[
d(x, y, z) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2 + (z_1 - z_2)^2}
\] I think you can already see the pattern. For every new dimension, we just need to sum the squared difference on the newly added axis, so the actual formula for a space with \(n\) dimensions becomes:
\[
d(p, q) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i - q_i)^2}
\]
And just like that, we can find the distance between any two concepts in our way-too-many dimensional space. In practice there are also other formulas for expressing how closely related two vectors are, such as Cosine Similarity which is what my code actually uses, but conceptually, the idea is not that different. Find out how related 2 mathematical expressions of meaning are.

title: Using Semantic Search for Dungeons and Dragons
text:
Putting it all together
So, how do we use all of this to find the relevant DnD spells?
For this purpose, we are going to use something called a Sentence Encoder, which is just a model that takes the text, segments it into tokens (each with an embedding) and then returns a single embedding corresponding to the overall meaning of the whole sequence. We are then going to find the vector that represents each of the spell descriptions in the rulebook and place all of them in a multi-dimensional space, just like the ones we discussed above. Then, once the user describes what they want to do, we will also find the vector representation for the input and place it in the same space. All we have left to do is to find the relation between the input vector and each of the spell description vectors and output the most closely related spells.
If you want to see the full program in action and play around with it, you can find it in the free tools section. Just beware, the server I am hosting it on is a bit slow and it may take a moment to load.
If you want to read through the source code, you can find all of it in the GitHub Repository.
If you would like to learn more about how sentence encoders (and other types of Large Language Models) update the meanings of individual tokens based on their context, check out my guide on Understanding Multi-Headed Self-Attention.

title: Understanding Multi-Headed Self-Attention
text:
MHSA is a core component of the Transformer architecture. The idea is that as the individual tokens, represented by Embeddings, come in, we need to find a contextual representation for each of them.
That is, the different meanings of stoned, in They stoned the witch. and This guy got completely stoned. need to be represented by different vectors, otherwise, we would be losing important semantic information.

title: Understanding Multi-Headed Self-Attention
text:
MHSA is a core component of the Transformer architecture. The idea is that as the individual tokens, represented by Embeddings, come in, we need to find a contextual representation for each of them.
That is, the different meanings of stoned, in They stoned the witch. and This guy got completely stoned. need to be represented by different vectors, otherwise, we would be losing important semantic information.

title: Understanding Multi-Headed Self-Attention
text:
How does it work?

High-level abstraction

The self-attention part
In order to achieve this change, we need to take into account the surrounding vectors in a learned manner. So, what we do is the following:

We create a table which can describe the relations between every pair of tokens by putting the full input sequence on both axes, like so:





Hello
world
!




Hello





world





!







Each vector will then ask the rest: ‘What do I interact with?’ and every vector, including itself, will say what does it interact with. What this actually means is that we will have 2 matrices, query (What do I interact with?), and key (I interact with these things!), which are going to multiply the vectors and create new vectors which will take their spots at the table, like so:





key(Hello)
key(world)
key(!)




query(Hello)





query(world)





query(!)






Note that queries take the rows, while keys take the columns.

Once this is done, we fill the cells with dot products of their corresponding row and column vectors. This can be understood as seeing if there is any compatibility between the ‘What do I interact with?’ and ‘I interact with these things!’ of the vectors.





key(Hello)
key(world)
key(!)




query(Hello)
11
16
19


query(world)
14
17
20


query(!)
15
18
21



I am obviously making the numbers up

However, we also need to divide them by the square root of the dimensionality of the qkv vectors, in order to keep the variance roughly around 1, independently of the model size. The resulting numbers are called the raw attention scores.











key(Hello)
key(world)
key(!)




query(Hello)
\(\frac{11}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{16}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{19}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)


query(world)
\(\frac{14}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{17}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{20}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)


query(!)
\(\frac{15}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{18}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)
\(\frac{21}{\sqrt{\text{d\_qkv}}}\)



I am obviously making the numbers up

And since the dot product is not restricted to anything and the numbers can vary an awful lot, we normalise them using Softmax row by row, which is going to return nice probability distributions of what interacts with what else. These numbers are called the (normalised) attention scores.





key(Hello)
key(world)
key(!)




query(Hello)
0.0
0.4
0.6


query(world)
0.9
0.05
0.05


query(!)
0.8
0.1
0.1



Didn’t actually apply softmax, still making up numbers

Once we have those, what we will do is that we will take the value matrices and we will use them to get yet another representation by multiplying the original embedding vectors. [That is, we will have value(Hello), value(world), value(!).] We will then multiply these representations in their corresponding columns by the (normalised) attention scores, like so:











key(Hello)
key(world)
key(!)




query(Hello)
\(0.0 \cdot value(Hello)\)
\(0.4 \cdot value(world)\)
\(0.6 \cdot value(!)\)


query(world)
\(0.9 \cdot value(Hello)\)
\(0.05 \cdot value(world)\)
\(0.05 \cdot value(!)\)


query(!)
\(0.8 \cdot value(Hello)\)
\(0.1 \cdot value(world)\)
\(0.1 \cdot value(!)\)



The resulting numbers are called attention weights

What we then do inside a transformer block is that for each row, we take the original embedding and sum it with whatever is in that row, like so: \[\text{updated\_Hello} = \text{Hello} + 0.0 \cdot value(Hello)+ 0.4 \cdot value(world) + 0.6 \cdot value(!)\] updated_Hello is the final contextual representation, Hello is the original input embedding, however, this is not technically part of the core attention mechanism, rather part of the transformer architecture, and it is therefore not done per head.



The multi-headed part
The multi-headed part of the name just means that we are doing multiple of the above operations in parallel, however, just how is it parallelised is quite clever:

We have the query, key and value representations, however, these often need to be quite big, so we split them into smaller chunks. That is, if these vectors have 30 columns and we want to have 10 heads, we would just split each of the matrices into 10 smaller ones, each ending up with 3 columns.
Then, what we do is that we do the above process in parallel for each of the heads and concatenate the outputs into one big vector (which happens to have the same dimensions as the token representation vector).
We then pass this vector through a linear transformation matrix and just like that, we have the output representation.

The idea behind this, aside from being efficient, is that it lets each of the heads specialise in something and do just that very well. We then slap those representations together and the pass through the linear transformation makes it so that the resulting vector is actually coherent, not just a bunch of small relationless representations.



The actual maths
In practice, we still have to do all of that, but we also need to worry about batches and multiple heads operating in parallel. Additionally, for efficiency reasons, we need to do everything via multi-dimensional tensor objects.
Here is the process, step by step:

We start with an input tensor of dimensions \([batch\_size, n\_tokens, embedding\_dim]\).
This gets multiplied by the three query, key and value matrices, each of dimensionality \([embedding\_dim, qkv\_dim]\), resulting in three new tensors, each of dimensionality \([batch\_size, n\_tokens, qkv\_dim]\). Each stores one of the 3 representations and I will be calling them queries, keys and values.
The last dimension then gets split into the heads, so the tensors end up with the following dimensions \([batch\_size, n\_tokens, n\_heads, head\_dim]\) where \(n\_heads\) is the number of heads and \(head\_dim\) is the dimensionality of each head, as explained above.
We then transpose the second and a third dimension, so that the dimensionality now looks like this: \([batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, head\_dim]\).
Now, we have all the tensors we want in the correct format, so we need to start using them. As explained above, we need to get the dot product of the queries and keys. To do this, we transpose the third and fourth dimensions of the keys tensor and multiply it with queries. That is, we are multiplying \(queries[batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, head\_dim] \cdot keys[batch\_size, n\_heads, head\_dim, n\_tokens]\). As mentioned in the previous step the first two dimensions \([batch\_size, n\_heads]\) sort of act as a 2-level nested loop, while the remaining two are essentially doing a matrix-matrix multiplication on every iteration of the inside loop with the following dimensionality: \([n\_tokens, head\_dim] \cdot [head\_dim, n\_tokens]\). This elegantly returns a matrix of \([n\_tokens, n\_tokens]\) dimensionality, that is, the self-attention matrix explained above, in the high-level section. The final dimensionality of the attention scores tensor is therefore \([batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, n\_tokens]\).
We then apply Softmax by row to this tensor divided by the square root of qkv dimensionality. (I am going to clarify, because there are a lot of dimensions floating around here, by qkv dimensionality, I mean the number dimensions of a single qkv vector in a single head. We divide by a scalar.)
We then multiply the attention scores tensor by the values tensor, that is, \(attn[batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, n\_tokens] \cdot values[batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, head\_dim]\). This returns the attention weights tensor, which has dimensions\([batch\_size, n\_heads, n\_tokens, head\_dim]\).
In order to extract the context vectors for the individual tokens from this tensor, we need to transpose back to the original tensor dimensionality, that is we transpose the second and third dimensions and attention weights becomes \([batch\_size, n\_tokens, n\_heads, head\_dim]\).
We then combine the heads back together and the dimensionality becomes \([batch\_size, n\_tokens, qkv\_dim]\).
We then multiply this by the linear projection matrix to make sure that the heads’ outputs actually work well together as a representation.
And thus, we end up with a tensor of contextualised representations where the last dimension is the dimension of the contextual representation with the same dimensionality as \(embeddin\_dim\).

title: Understanding the Viterbi algorithm
text:
The Viterbi algorithm is used for calculating the most likely sequence of events in a Hidden Markov Model.
As a bit of a reminder, in this kind of model, what we do is that we have a Markov chain which we cannot observe, however, there are also events which we can observe which depend on the states of the HMM.
Having said that, what we theoretically could do would be to would be to take all the possible combinations of states which could lead to the observed events, get the likelihood of each of those combinations and see which combination reaches the highest value. However, this is incredibly inefficient, so, here is where the Viterbi algorithm comes in. It reaches the same result as comparing all the possible combinations, it just does it in a clever way.

title: Understanding the Viterbi algorithm
text:
How does it work?
Assume we have the following table of transition log probabilities in the Markov chain:




Noun
Verb
ENDTOKEN




STARTTOKEN
\(-1\)
\(-2\)
\(-\infty\)


Noun
\(-3\)
\(-1\)
\(-4\)


Verb
\(-1\)

\(-1\)



And the following table for the observable events that depend on the Markov chain states:




They
can
fish




Noun
-2
-3
-3


Verb
-10

-3



Now, we can take a look at a sentence:

They can fish.

What is the most likely sequence of states (Parts of speech) that could have lead to this sequence.
Using the Viterbi algorithm, we can do the following:

First we examine the probability of the first word belonging to any of the classes. This is, the probability of the class following a STARTTOKEN, times the probability of the class.





They




Noun
\(-1-2=-3\)


Verb
\(-2 -10 = -12\)




Now, we have the probability of They being each of those classes. We need to incorporate this into the calculation of the next word.

In particular, we now have to juggle 3 probabilities. The probability of the previous tag, the probability of the current tag given the previous tag and the probability of the current tag given the word. (In this order in the table below).






They
can




Noun
\(-3\)
\(-3-3-3=-9\) | \(-12-1-3=-14\)


Verb
\(-12\)
\(-3-1-1=-5\) | \(-12-3-1=-16\)



Doing this gets us various probabilities per cell. We simply take the highest one, note down the assumption about previous tag that lead us to it and repeat until the table is full.




They
can
fish




Noun
\(-3\)
-9 (from noun)
\(-9 -3 -3 = -15\)|\(-5 -1 -3 = -9\)


Verb
\(-12\)
-5 (from noun)
\(-9 -1 -3 = -13\)|\(-5 -3 -3 =-11\)



Now, for the end token, we take just the probability of it following a specific pos tag times the probability of that pos tag. We aren’t assigning it any tag, so there is no need for multiple cells in that last column, I just don’t know how to do that in Obsidian.











They
can
fish
END TOKEN




Noun
\(-3\)
-9 (from noun)
\(-9\) (from noun)
\(-9 -4 = -13\) | \(-11 - 1 = -12\)


Verb
\(-12\)
-5 (from noun)
\(-11\) (from verb)




Once this is done, we once again take the highest probability and note down where it came from.











They
can
fish
END TOKEN




Noun
\(-3\)
-9 (from noun)
\(-9\) (from noun)
\(-12\) (from verb)


Verb
\(-12\)
-5 (from noun)
\(-11\) (from verb)




Once this table is complete, what we do is that we start from the end and follow the arrows all the way to the beginning. That is, we got the best probability for the end token from a verb, so we assume that the last tag was a verb. Then, we look at the column corresponding to that token and the cell corresponding to the verb tag. Where did we get the best probability for that cell? From the verb tag. So we go to the previous and repeat until we have found the most probable sequence.











They
can
fish
END TOKEN

-3
\(-9\) (from noun)
\(-9\) (from noun)
-12 (from verb)

\(-12\)
-5 (from noun)
-11 (from verb)




Therefore, the most likely sequence of tags would be the following: \[[[\text{NOUN}]], [[\text{VERB}]], [[\text{VERB}]]\]

title: Spanish Present Tense Searcher
section: How does it work on the inside?
text:
How does it work on the inside?
The program works in two stages: First, an HMM tagger trained on the AnCora corpus tags the sentences using the Universal Dependencies PoS tags. It achieves 94.74% overall accuracy and f1 score for the VERB tag of 0.9185. In the second stage, a complex regex pattern (below) is used to separate present tenses from all the other tenses. The sentences determined to contain at least one present tense are then saved and printed.
The regex pattern: [a-záéíóúñA-ZÁÉÍÓÚÑ]+((?<!(ad)|(id)|(and))o|(?<!(ab)|(í)|(ar))as|(?<!(ab)|(í)|(ar))a|(?<!(ab)|(í)|(ár))amos|áis|(?<!(ab)|(í)|(ar))an|[^s]es|[^s]e|[^rs]emos|[^r]éis|[^s]en|imos|ís|y){1}$
